Let the grid be denoted by $G$. The grid has $5$ rows and $5$ columns.
We are given that each cell contains at most one chip.
All chips in the same row have the same color.
All chips in the same column have the same color.
Any additional chip placed on the grid would violate one or more of the previous two conditions.

Let's consider the conditions carefully.
Condition 1: Each cell contains at most one chip. This means we are either placing a chip or not placing a chip in each cell.
Condition 2: All chips in the same row have the same color. This implies that if a row has any chips, all chips in that row must be of the same color. It also implies that if a row has chips of one color, it cannot have chips of the other color. This further means that a row can either be all white chips, all black chips, or empty.
Condition 3: All chips in the same column have the same color. Similar to the row condition, this means a column can either be all white chips, all black chips, or empty.

Condition 4: Any additional chip placed on the grid would violate one or more of the previous two conditions. This condition is a bit tricky. Let's consider what it means.

Let's analyze the implications of the first three conditions on the coloring of the grid.
Suppose row $i$ contains chips. Then all chips in row $i$ must be of the same color, say $C_i$.
Suppose column $j$ contains chips. Then all chips in column $j$ must be of the same color, say $K_j$.

Now consider a cell $(i, j)$.
If cell $(i, j)$ contains a chip, its color is determined by the color of row $i$ and the color of column $j$.
If row $i$ has chips, they are all color $C_i$.
If column $j$ has chips, they are all color $K_j$.
If cell $(i, j)$ has a chip, and it's part of row $i$ with chips and column $j$ with chips, then the color of the chip must be both $C_i$ and $K_j$. This means that if a row and a column both contain chips, and the cell at their intersection has a chip, the color of that chip is uniquely determined.

Let's consider the coloring of the rows and columns.
For each row, we can decide if it is empty, all white, or all black.
For each column, we can decide if it is empty, all white, or all black.

Let $R_i$ denote row $i$, and $C_j$ denote column $j$.
Let the color of row $i$ be $color(R_i) \in \{W, B, \text{empty}\}$.
Let the color of column $j$ be $color(C_j) \in \{W, B, \text{empty}\}$.

If cell $(i, j)$ has a chip, then its color must be consistent with the row color and column color.
If $color(R_i) = W$ and $color(C_j) = W$, then cell $(i, j)$ can have a white chip.
If $color(R_i) = B$ and $color(C_j) = B$, then cell $(i, j)$ can have a black chip.
If $color(R_i) = W$ and $color(C_j) = B$, then cell $(i, j)$ cannot have a chip of either color that is consistent with both. So, if a row is entirely white and a column is entirely black, any cell at their intersection cannot contain a chip. This implies that if $color(R_i) \neq \text{empty}$ and $color(C_j) \neq \text{empty}$, then it must be that $color(R_i) = color(C_j)$ for cell $(i, j)$ to contain a chip.

This means that if a row is non-empty, and a column is non-empty, they must have the same color for any chips to be at their intersection.

For any $i \in I_R$ and $j \in I_C$, if cell $(i, j)$ contains a chip, then $color(R_i) = color(C_j)$.
